usage: softer, more poetic cousin of 달다, used for desserts and even romance
the noun 단맛 (sweet + taste) is how you name the flavor itself
꿀처럼 is the go-to simile for intense sweetness
to be tasty / to keep saying
idiom: food is delicious, or a word is 'always on your lips'
examples: 이 사탕 정말 달아요.
This candy is really sweet.
plain statement with 정말 for emphasis; note the subject takes 이
딸기가 생각보다 달아서 깜짝 놀랐어요.
The strawberries were sweeter than expected, so I was surprised.
-아서 links the taste to your reaction
손님, 단거 좋아하시면 이 케이크 추천드려요.
If you like sweet things, sir, I recommend this cake.
shop register: 단거 = 단 것 (sweet thing), 추천드리다 is humble
nuance: 달다 is the basic word for sugary, honey-like sweetness, and the dividing line you must learn is 달다 vs 달콤하다: 달다 is the flat, factual report ('this is sweet, maybe too sweet'), while 달콤하다 adds a warm, pleasant, almost romantic glow ('sweet and lovely') and is preferred for desserts, perfume, even 달콤한 사랑. As an adjective 달다 takes 이/가 on the thing tasted (커피가 달아요), never 을/를. Watch the irregular conjugation: the stem ends in ㄹ, which drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ — so the formal form is 답니다 (not 달습니다) and the modifier is 단 (단 음식), yet 달아요 keeps the ㄹ. The English-speaker trap is twofold: do not write 다라요, and remember that to 'add sugar' uses a verb (설탕을 넣다), because English 'sweeten' has no one-word match here. 달다 also coexists with the unrelated verb 달다 meaning 'to hang/attach', so context decides.

mistakes: Saying '이 커피를 달아요' — 달다 is descriptive, so the tasted item is the subject with 이/가: 이 커피가 달아요.
Writing the polite form as 다라요; the correct contraction keeps the block as 달아요.
Using the formal 달습니다 — because of ㄹ-dropping it must be 답니다.

usage: 신맛 (sour + taste) names the flavor; 나다 means the taste 'comes out'
vivid variant of 시다, hints at a slightly off or fermented sour smell too
the GOOD sour — bright and appetizing, as in 새콤달콤 (sweet-and-sour)
식초 (vinegar) is the benchmark for sharp sourness
examples: 레몬이 너무 셔요.
The lemon is too sour.
basic taste report; 너무 = too (much)
김치가 익어서 좀 셔요.
The kimchi has fermented, so it's a little sour.
-아서 ties fermentation to the sourness; 익다 = to ripen/ferment
이거 상했나 봐요, 우유에서 신맛이 나요.
I think this has gone bad — the milk tastes sour.
real situation: sour milk signals spoilage, using 신맛이 나다
nuance: 시다 is the sharp, acidic taste of lemon, vinegar, or over-fermented kimchi, and the key contrast is 시다 vs 새콤하다: 시다 is neutral-to-negative (it can simply mean 'too sour' or even 'spoiled'), whereas 새콤하다 is always the pleasant, refreshing tang you want in 새콤달콤 sweet-and-sour dishes. As a description the sour thing takes 이/가 (레몬이 셔요). The conjugation is the real pitfall: the stem 시- meets the 어요 ending and contracts, so the polite form is 셔요 (시+어요 → 셔요) and the past is 셨어요 — many learners wrongly write the uncontracted 시어요, which sounds bookish and unnatural in speech. Also note Koreans say a sour smell or spoiled food 시다/시큼하다, so when milk goes off you say 신맛이 나다 rather than translating 'gone bad' literally. Keep the subject particle 이/가 and never attach 을/를 to the tasted item.

mistakes: Saying 시어요 in conversation — the natural contracted form is 셔요 (and past 셨어요).
Attaching 을/를: '레몬을 셔요' is wrong; the sour thing is the subject, 레몬이 셔요.
Confusing 시다 with 매콤하다/맵다; 시다 is acidic-sour, not spicy-hot.

usage: 짠맛 (salty + taste) is the noun for the flavor itself
간 = the salt level of a dish; 간이 짜다/싱겁다 is how cooks judge food
adverb 짜게 + 먹다; doctors warn 짜게 먹지 마세요 (don't eat salty)
examples: 국이 좀 짜요.
The soup is a bit salty.
everyday complaint at the table; 좀 softens it
라면을 끓일 때 스프를 다 넣으면 짜요.
If you add the whole seasoning packet when cooking ramen, it gets salty.
-(으)면 condition → result
사장님이 좀 짠 편이라 회식을 잘 안 사요.
The boss is a bit stingy, so he rarely treats us to dinner.
real-life slang: 짜다 = tightfisted, not about taste
nuance: 짜다 means having a strong salt taste, and the practical contrast for cooking is 짜다 vs 간이 맞다: 짜다 says there is too much salt, while 간이 맞다 means the seasoning is just right (and 싱겁다 means too little). The salty thing takes 이/가 (국이 짜요). Conjugation is regular for an ㅏ-stem: 짜 + 아요 contracts to 짜요 (not 짜아요), past 짰어요. Two pitfalls for English speakers: first, never write 짜아요. Second, 짜다 has a very common figurative meaning — 'stingy / tightfisted' — so 그 사람 진짜 짜 means 'that person is so cheap', nothing to do with food; English 'salty' meaning 'bitter/annoyed' does NOT transfer to Korean 짜다, so do not use it that way. When you want to talk about how salty you eat in general, use the adverb 짜게 (짜게 먹다), which health advice constantly repeats.

mistakes: Writing 짜아요 for the polite form; the ㅏ-stem contracts to 짜요.
Using 짜다 to mean emotionally 'salty/annoyed' as in English — in Korean that figurative sense is 'stingy', so the English idiom does not carry over.
Saying '이 국을 짜요' — the dish is the subject: 이 국이 짜요.

usage: the standard cook's verdict opposite 간이 짜다
맛이 + 싱겁다 reports a weak overall flavor
figurative: someone whose jokes or actions fall flat
examples: 국이 좀 싱거워요.
The soup is a bit bland.
table comment; 좀 keeps it polite
소금을 안 넣어서 찌개가 싱거워요.
I didn't add salt, so the stew is bland.
-아서 cause; pairs the missing salt with the result
병원 밥은 싱겁게 나와서 처음엔 입에 안 맞았어요.
Hospital food comes lightly seasoned, so at first it didn't suit my taste.
real situation with 싱겁게 and 입에 맞다
nuance: 싱겁다 is the exact opposite of 짜다: it means a dish lacks salt or has too weak a flavor. The contrast to fix is 싱겁다 vs 담백하다 — both describe mild food, but 싱겁다 is a complaint ('underseasoned, needs salt') while 담백하다 is praise ('cleanly light, refreshing'); never mix them up when complimenting a cook. The bland thing takes 이/가 (국이 싱거워요). This is a ㅂ-irregular: before a vowel ending the ㅂ becomes 우, so 싱겁 + 어요 → 싱거워요, past 싱거웠어요, modifier 싱거운; the formal form keeps ㅂ as 싱겁습니다. The English-speaker trap is writing the regular 싱겁어요 — that form does not exist. Like several taste words it has a figurative use: a person or a story can be 싱겁다, meaning 'anticlimactic, a let-down', as in 그 영화 결말 좀 싱거웠어 ('the ending was a bit flat').

Calling underseasoned food 담백하다 to be polite — 담백하다 is praise, but if it truly lacks salt the honest word is 싱겁다.
Saying '이 국을 싱거워요' — the dish is the subject: 이 국이 싱거워요.

usage: the most common modifier pairing; 뜨거운 + noun
김 = steam; you often warn 뜨거우니까 김 조심하세요
figurative: intense passion or public attention
examples: 커피가 아직 뜨거워요.
The coffee is still hot.
everyday; 아직 = still
방금 끓여서 국이 너무 뜨거워요, 조심하세요.
I just boiled it, so the soup is very hot — be careful.
-아서 cause + warning 조심하세요
뜨거운 거 못 드시면 조금 식혀서 드릴게요.
If you can't handle hot things, I'll let it cool a bit before serving.
service register: 드시다/드리다 honorifics with 식히다
nuance: 뜨겁다 describes high temperature you feel by touch or in the mouth — hot soup, hot coffee — and the crucial contrast for English speakers is 뜨겁다 vs 맵다: English 'hot' covers both temperature and spice, but Korean splits them, so a fiery chili dish is 맵다 (spicy), never 뜨겁다. Use 뜨겁다 only for heat. The hot thing takes 이/가 (커피가 뜨거워요). It is a ㅂ-irregular verb: 뜨겁 + 어요 → 뜨거워요, past 뜨거웠어요, modifier 뜨거운 (뜨거운 물), but formal 뜨겁습니다 keeps the ㅂ. Compare with 따뜻하다 (pleasantly warm): 뜨겁다 is so hot it can burn, while 따뜻하다 is comfortably warm — choose by degree. Figuratively, 뜨겁다 means passionate or intense (뜨거운 관심, 뜨거운 응원). Avoid the made-up form 뜨겁어요.

Writing 뜨겁어요; the ㅂ-irregular form is 뜨거워요.
Confusing 뜨겁다 (burning hot) with 따뜻하다 (comfortably warm) — they differ by intensity.

usage: 얼음 (ice) as the benchmark for sharp cold
examples: 물이 정말 차가워요.
The water is really cold.
basic; 정말 emphasizes
냉장고에 넣어 둬서 주스가 시원하게 차가워요.
I kept it in the fridge, so the juice is refreshingly cold.
-아서 cause + 시원하게 nuance
그 사람 첫인상은 좀 차가웠는데 알고 보니 따뜻한 사람이에요.
He seemed a bit cold at first, but he turned out to be warm.
figurative contrast 차갑다 vs 따뜻하다 about personality
nuance: 차갑다 describes a cold temperature felt by touch — cold water, an iced drink, cold hands. The contrast to master is 차갑다 vs 시원하다: 차갑다 is plainly, even uncomfortably cold (object-temperature), while 시원하다 is the pleasant, refreshing cool you welcome on a hot day or in a cold drink, and it does not transfer to people. The cold thing takes 이/가 (물이 차가워요). It is a ㅂ-irregular: 차갑 + 어요 → 차가워요, past 차가웠어요, modifier 차가운, but formal 차갑습니다 keeps ㅂ. There is also a near-twin 춥다 (to be cold): use 춥다 only for the weather/air you feel as a person (날씨가 추워요), and 차갑다 for objects you touch (물이 차가워요) — mixing them is the classic learner error. Figuratively 차갑다 means cold-hearted or aloof (차가운 표정, 차가운 말투). Avoid the wrong form 차갑어요.

Writing 차갑어요; the ㅂ-irregular polite form is 차가워요.
Replacing 차갑다 with 시원하다 for an unpleasantly cold object — 시원하다 implies it feels good/refreshing.

usage: 식감 = texture; the standard food-review phrase
vivid idiom: 입에서 살살 녹아요 (melts in your mouth)
adverb 부드럽게 + 말하다; soft manner of speaking
examples: 이 빵이 정말 부드러워요.
This bread is really soft.
basic food praise
고기를 푹 익혀서 부드러워요.
I cooked the meat thoroughly, so it's tender.
-아서 cause; 푹 익히다 = cook well
목소리가 부드러워서 듣기 편했어요.
His voice was soft, so it was easy to listen to.
figurative: 부드럽다 about voice/manner
nuance: 부드럽다 covers a smooth, gentle softness — soft bread, tender meat, smooth fabric, even a gentle voice or manner. The contrast you need is 부드럽다 vs 말랑하다: 부드럽다 is broad and refined (smooth, mellow, gentle), while 말랑하다 specifically means squishy-springy to the touch like a marshmallow or 말랑한 젤리; for tender, melt-in-the-mouth food Koreans prefer 부드럽다. The soft thing takes 이/가 (빵이 부드러워요). It is ㅂ-irregular: 부드럽 + 어요 → 부드러워요, past 부드러웠어요, modifier 부드러운, but formal 부드럽습니다 keeps ㅂ. A useful opposite is 딱딱하다 (hard, stiff). Note the strong figurative range: 부드러운 사람 (a gentle person), 부드러운 말투 (a soft tone) — unlike English 'soft', this is a compliment about character, not weakness. Avoid the invalid form 부드럽어요.

Saying '이 빵을 부드러워요' — the food is the subject: 이 빵이 부드러워요.

usage: 돌 (stone) as the benchmark for stale bread, etc.
figurative: rigid, unfriendly way of speaking
examples: 이 과자가 너무 딱딱해요.
This cracker is too hard.
basic texture complaint
빵이 식어서 딱딱해졌어요.
The bread cooled down and got hard.
-아서 cause + 해지다 (become); change of state
회의 분위기가 너무 딱딱해서 농담 한마디 했어요.
The meeting felt so stiff that I cracked a joke.
figurative use about atmosphere
nuance: 딱딱하다 describes a stiff, unyielding hardness — stale bread, a hard chair, frozen-solid food. The contrast to know is 딱딱하다 vs 질기다: 딱딱하다 means rigid and crunchy-hard (it cracks), while 질기다 means tough and chewy (it stretches and resists your teeth, like overcooked squid or gristly meat) — beginners often say 딱딱하다 when they mean 질기다. As a description the hard thing takes 이/가 (과자가 딱딱해요). It follows the regular 하다 pattern: 딱딱하 + 여요 → 딱딱해요, past 딱딱했어요, modifier 딱딱한, formal 딱딱합니다. The opposite for food is 부드럽다. Figuratively 딱딱하다 means stiff or overly formal — 딱딱한 분위기 (a stiff atmosphere), 딱딱한 사람 (an inflexible person) — and the onomatopoeic doubling 딱딱 gives it that hard, knocking feel. Avoid the form 딱딱하요 (the 하다 ending is 해요).

usage: 재료 = ingredients; a staple cooking/marketing phrase
신선도 (freshness level, 度 = degree) is the measurable noun
figurative: a pleasantly surprising, novel impression
examples: 이 우유가 신선해요.
This milk is fresh.
basic; product freshness
오늘 아침에 들어와서 생선이 신선해요.
It came in this morning, so the fish is fresh.
-아서 cause; market situation
발상이 정말 신선하네요, 그런 생각은 못 했어요.

The contrast to master is 신선하다 vs 싱싱하다: 신선하다 is the broad, slightly formal word (also used figuratively for ideas), while 싱싱하다 is the lively, native-Korean word that specifically evokes plump, vibrant, still-alive freshness — a fish flapping at the market is 싱싱하다 more than 신선하다. The big English-speaker pitfall: 'fresh' in English also means cheeky/impertinent and cool weather — neither transfers; Korean 신선하다 is purely about freshness/novelty. For a refreshing breeze use 시원하다 instead. Figuratively 신선한 충격 means a pleasantly novel surprise.

usage: the core descriptor for sesame/nut taste
고소하다 describes aroma as well as taste
figurative slang: smug pleasure at someone's misfortune
examples: 이 빵에서 고소한 맛이 나요.
This bread has a nutty flavor.
basic; 맛이 나다 for 'taste comes out'
참기름을 살짝 둘러서 더 고소해요.
I drizzled a little sesame oil, so it's even nuttier.
-아서 cause; 참기름 is the prototypical 고소한 oil
미운 사람이 혼나니까 좀 고소하더라.
It was kind of satisfying to see that annoying person get scolded.
figurative/slang 고소하다 = schadenfreude, with -더라
nuance: 고소하다 names a flavor English barely has a single word for: the warm, toasty, savory taste/aroma of roasted sesame, peanuts, perilla, nuts, and grains — think 참기름, 들기름, 콩가루. The contrast to learn is 고소하다 vs 구수하다: 고소하다 is the bright, light roasted-sesame note, while 구수하다 is a deeper, earthier roasted warmth (well-brewed 숭늉/누룽지, soybean paste 된장, barley tea) — they overlap but 구수하다 feels heartier and more rustic. There is no Sino-Korean root; it is native Korean. The tasty thing takes 이/가 (빵이 고소해요) or you say X에서 고소한 맛이 나다. Regular 하다 conjugation: 고소해요, past 고소했어요, modifier 고소한, formal 고소합니다. English-speaker pitfall: 'nutty' is only an approximation — do not restrict 고소하다 to literal nuts, and beware its common slang meaning 'serves you right / I'm secretly glad', a sense pure English 'nutty' never carries.

usage: the default modifier; fried or fatty dishes
속 (stomach) + 느끼하다: the heavy, sickly feeling
느끼함 (the greasiness) + 잡다; e.g. 김치가 느끼함을 잡아줘요
figurative: an over-the-top flirty or corny remark
examples: 이 피자가 좀 느끼해요.
This pizza is a bit greasy.
basic; 좀 softens the complaint
기름진 고기를 많이 먹어서 속이 느끼해요.
I ate a lot of fatty meat, so I feel queasy.
-아서 cause; 속이 느끼하다 = stomach feels heavy
그 사람 자꾸 느끼한 말 해서 좀 부담스러웠어요.
He kept saying cheesy lines, so it felt a bit much.
figurative 느끼하다 = corny/cringey, with 부담스럽다
nuance: 느끼하다 describes the heavy, oily, cloying feeling of fatty food — pizza, cream pasta, deep-fried meat — and crucially also the queasy after-feeling in your stomach (속이 느끼하다). The contrast to fix is 느끼하다 vs 기름지다: 기름지다 neutrally states a dish is oily/rich (it can even be appetizing), while 느끼하다 carries the negative 'too rich, makes me want something to cut it' nuance — that's why Koreans say 느끼할 때 김치/콜라가 필요해. Its opposite is 담백하다 (cleanly light). The greasy thing takes 이/가 (피자가 느끼해요). Regular 하다 conjugation: 느끼해요, past 느끼했어요, modifier 느끼한, formal 느끼합니다. Big English-speaker pitfall: 'greasy' is only half the meaning — 느끼하다 is also the standard way to call a person or their words 'cheesy / corny / smarmy' (느끼한 멘트, 느끼한 남자), so a slick flirt is 느끼하다, which surprises learners expecting only a food word.

usage: the praise phrase for non-greasy taste
기름기 (oiliness) + 없다; what makes food 담백하다
examples: 이 두부 요리가 담백해요.
This tofu dish is light and clean.
basic praise for mild food
기름을 안 써서 담백하고 깔끔해요.
It's made without oil, so it's light and clean-tasting.
-아서 cause; 담백하다 + 깔끔하다 pairing
그 배우는 인터뷰에서 늘 담백하게 말해서 호감이에요.
That actor always speaks plainly in interviews, which makes him likeable.
figurative 담백하다 about a frank manner
nuance: 담백하다 is Sino-Korean from 淡白 (淡 'thin/light in taste' + 白 'plain/white'), and it is the praise-word for food that tastes clean and mild without grease or heavy seasoning — white fish, tofu, chicken breast, clear broth. It is the deliberate opposite of 느끼하다 (cloyingly greasy). The contrast to master is 담백하다 vs 싱겁다: both describe non-strong flavor, but 담백하다 is a compliment ('refreshingly clean, light'), while 싱겁다 is a complaint ('underseasoned, needs salt') — so call good light food 담백하다, never 싱겁다. The food takes 이/가 (두부 요리가 담백해요). Regular 하다 conjugation: 담백해요, past 담백했어요, modifier 담백한, formal 담백합니다. English-speaker pitfall: do not translate with plain 'light' as in low-calorie or pale-colored — 담백하다 is specifically about a clean, non-greasy taste. Figuratively it also praises a frank, unpretentious personality (담백한 사람).
